name: Amira Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Amira. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check health insurance claims at a private health insurer, the ones the system flags as odd: a physio clinic billing twenty sessions in a week, a dental bill that doesn't match the X-ray notes. I pull the records, compare them, sometimes call the clinic, and decide whether to pay, query or pass it to the fraud team. I've been there six years, and I run half my checks through an AI assistant before I even open the file.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like catching the patterns, like noticing three clinics using the same wording on their invoices. What wears me out is the false alarms: most flags are just a tired receptionist making a typo. Outside work I buy old film cameras, fix them up at my kitchen table and sell them online, which is my favourite part of the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a bit of a letdown, honestly, but a comfortable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got overhyped, and that people who learned it still got a lot out of it. Online I'd post a couple of the ways I use it. At work I'd say let's keep improving the flag rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my job is safe and I'm a bit faster than most of my colleagues. The routine stuff it automates is already the stuff I've handed to it. If AI never gets better than this, I've already squeezed out most of what it can do for a claims checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep investing a slice of my pay every month, and grow the camera business a bit. Maybe ask for a move onto the fraud team, which pays more. Nothing drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the camera business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. Maybe fifteen cameras a month, enough for a nice holiday a year. I like that it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Health insurers always need people who can read clinical notes, and there are three other insurers in town hiring.

steps.text: Keep investing part of each payslip in index funds
Grow the film camera repair business to twenty cameras a month
Apply for an opening on the fraud team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels like what's already happening at my insurer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn the tools now rather than wait to be told, and that the change can be good if it's handled well. At work I'd offer to train others. Online I'd share tips without preaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the checker team shrinks a lot, but I'm in good shape because I already work this way. The ones who won't adapt are in trouble. I'm not worried about AI replacing me this year; I'm worried about being the only person left to check what the AI flagged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move into reviewing the AI's decisions, the oversight role, before it's advertised. I'd take a short course on how these models make mistakes. I'd keep investing and keep the cameras going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, but for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham, who's fifty-eight and does everything on paper first. He's careful and good, but he'd hate the new way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it can be good. Good for whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, probably, and for patients if claims get paid faster. Less good for people like Graham. I try to hold both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That would actually shake me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving too fast for any company to manage, and the government needs to slow the rollout. I'd say it at work too. People would be surprised, because I'm usually the AI fan in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the oversight role I'd aim for disappears as well, because an AI that thinks like a person can check another AI. Being good with AI buys me a year, maybe two, and then I'm a claims checker in a world that doesn't need claims checkers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job while it lasts and save harder. I'd turn the camera business into a proper repair shop, since hands-on work gets three more years. And I'd move some investments into safer things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have savings and a plan, but the plan's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the plan thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because fixing cameras is lovely, but it pays a holiday, not a rent. I'd need it to triple, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move anywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe back near my parents, where rent's half. I'd hate it, but I'd do it if the shop needed a year to grow.

fieldNote: Amira's AI fluency **stops protecting** her under fast AGI.

steps.text: Save an extra quarter of each payslip while employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more like it. I can work with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but we've got time, so let's use it well. At work I'd push for the company to plan transitions. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get three or four good years in oversight work, well paid, then it fades. That's enough to build the camera shop properly. Five years is the sweet spot for me: long enough to save from a good salary, short enough to stop me getting lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the oversight role in year one and bank the pay. I'd build the camera business on weekends, aiming to make it a full shop by year four. I'd keep investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I was driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot delay matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Camera repair is fiddly hands-on work. Even when robots arrive around 2034, I doubt anyone builds one for old film cameras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they should have a hands-on hobby they could turn into money. Most of them laugh at me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade and people should start learning now. At work I'd be the one running lunch sessions. Online I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I ride this well. Oversight work for years, the camera shop growing, savings building. Ten years of warning with my savings and a skill in my hands sounds less like a threat and more like a schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the oversight role, keep investing, and grow the camera shop slowly. Maybe buy a small flat with a ground-floor room for the shop around year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit excited about the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Health. If I couldn't use my hands, the plan falls apart. That's the honest weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever has the most sensible plan for retraining and keeps the shops and small businesses going. That's always been my vote.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is time and small-business help, like cheap loans to open a repair shop. People talk about AI as if everyone sits at a screen, but my backup plan is a screwdriver and a box of old cameras.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about hobbies. I think the people who'll do best have something they're good at with their hands.

headlineQuote: People talk about AI as if everyone sits at a screen, but my backup plan is a screwdriver and a box of old cameras.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** health insurance claims checker who uses AI every day.
She runs a small **film camera repair** business from her kitchen.
She's **pragmatic** and sees AI as good for her but hard on colleagues.
Her plan moves from **oversight work** to a full repair shop.
She feels **calm** or uneasy in most pictures, and **anxious** only if AGI comes by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her camera shop wouldn't have time to grow.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, plus small-business help like **cheap loans** for a repair shop.
